The question this section leaves open

slides.title: Memory *architectures*
slides.text: What does an agent remember, and how far does it hold?

narration: An AI agent forgets everything when its task ends.
Unless something is built to remember for it.
That something is called its memory.
This section looks at how memories are built today.
It looks at how they are scored.
And it asks how far the scores are from what an enterprise needs.

slides.caption: Memory is what an agent keeps between tasks. This section looks at how memories are built and scored. It asks how far the scores are from what an enterprise needs.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: Why memory is its own subject
Six ways to build a memory

narration: This section has six pages.
Each page is a run of slides like this one.
Each slide is explained under it, in plain words.
First, why memory needs its own section.
Then the six ways a memory can be built.
Then how memory systems are scored, and where the scores mislead.
Then why a one-million-token context window is not a memory.
Then the question that gives the section its point.
It is about ten million tokens.
Last, the one system we tested ourselves.

slides.caption: Six pages. Why memory needs its own section, six ways to build one, and how memory is scored. Then long context, the ten-million-token question, and what we measured.

slides.title: An agent forgets when the task *ends*
slides.text: The model keeps nothing between calls.

narration: At the heart of any AI system is a model.
It reads text and writes text back.
A system that uses a model to do a job is called an agent.
The model keeps nothing between calls.
When the task ends, everything it saw is gone.
The next task starts from a blank page.
For a chat about the weather, that is fine.
For a claims team or a service desk, it is not.
They need the agent to remember last week, last year, and the customer's whole history.

slides.caption: A model reads text and writes text. An agent is a system that uses a model to do a job. When the job ends, the model keeps nothing.

slides.title: That something is its *memory*
slides.text: A store, an index, and a way back to the right piece.

narration: Memory is what is built around the model to remember for it.
It is a store, an index, and a way to bring the right piece back.
It is not part of the model.
What the store keeps decides what can ever be recalled.
How the index works decides what is found.
Those two choices are the subject of this section.
This guide already says what a memory must carry.
Its source, its permissions, and a working delete.
This section adds how it is built, and whether the build works.

slides.caption: Memory is what is built around the model so the agent can recall. It is a store, an index, and a way to bring the right piece back.

slides.title: A crowded *field*
slides.unit: named memory systems, four cloud services, six taxonomies, ten new benchmarks
slides.text: Every one reports a score. Almost none compare.

narration: By September 2026 there are more than thirty named memory systems.
Four large cloud providers ship a managed memory service.
Six survey papers propose their own taxonomy.
Since 2025 at least ten new benchmarks have appeared.
Every system reports a score on one of them.
Almost none of the scores can be compared with each other.
The judges differ.
The question subsets differ.
And the sizes of the tests are far below what an enterprise runs at.

slides.caption: By September 2026 there are more than thirty named memory systems and four managed cloud services. Six survey taxonomies and ten new benchmarks. Almost none of their scores compare.

slides.title: Two facts decide *everything*

narration: The first fact is what is stored.
Original words, a summary, extracted facts, a graph, or the weights.
What is stored decides what can ever be found again.
The second fact is when a model runs.
At write time, as each document arrives.
At read time, as each question comes in.
In the background, between tasks.
Or during training, so the memory lives in the weights.
Those two facts decide the cost, and they decide what is lost.
Page two sorts every named system by them.

slides.caption: Every memory architecture is placed by what it stores and by when a model runs. Those two choices fix what can be recalled and what it costs.

slides.title: Every high score is *small*
slides.text: Above 90 percent was earned on 16 to 115 thousand tokens.

narration: Vendors report scores in the low nineties on the two best-known benchmarks.
Those scores are real, under the judges the vendors chose.
But look at the size of the test.
The smaller benchmark has conversations of 16 to 26 thousand tokens.
The larger one has about 115 thousand tokens per question.
A modern model reads either of those in one call.
So a high score there says little about memory at scale.
Page three shows what the benchmarks measure and where scores mislead.

slides.caption: Every memory score above 90 percent was earned on a conversation of 16 thousand to 115 thousand tokens. That fits inside one call to a modern model.

slides.title: Ten million *tokens*
slides.unit: tokens is a little more than one year of one worker's received mail and chat
slides.text: An enterprise memory starts there and grows every day.

narration: A token is the unit AI usage is measured in.
It is roughly three quarters of a word.
Ten million tokens is about seven million words.
That is a little more than one year of one worker's received mail and chat.
Before any attachments, documents, tickets or meetings.
A customer's history over a decade is larger.
A litigation file is larger.
A plant's maintenance record is larger.
Ten million is the floor for an enterprise memory, not the ceiling.

slides.caption: Ten million tokens is a little more than one year of one worker's received mail and chat. An enterprise memory workload starts there and grows.

slides.title: At ten million, the best *result*
slides.text: No commercial memory system was evaluated by the authors.

narration: One public benchmark reaches ten million tokens.
It is called BEAM, and it was published at a top conference in 2026.
At that size, giving the model everything scores 0.10 on a scale of 0 to 1.
Finding the best pieces first and passing them in scores 0.25.
The benchmark authors built their own memory design.
It scores 0.27.
That is the best published, independently run result at ten million tokens.
Nothing is close to solid.

slides.caption: One public benchmark reaches ten million tokens. There, plain long context scores 0.10 and retrieval 0.25. The authors' own memory design scores 0.27 on a scale of 0 to 1.

slides.title: Vendor numbers at ten million are *unchecked*
slides.text: Own judge, own harness, not reproduced.

narration: Three vendors have since published their own ten-million-token numbers.
Each used its own judge and its own test harness.
None of them is comparable to the paper's table.
None is comparable to the others.
None has been reproduced by anyone else.
This section shows them, flagged as vendor reported.
It never places them in a ranking.

slides.caption: Three vendors have published their own ten-million-token scores. Each used its own judge and harness. None is comparable to the paper, and none has been reproduced.

slides.title: Three rules for every *number*
items: Independent numbers in their own rows

narration: This section handles numbers under three rules.
First, a number from the party that built the system is flagged as vendor reported.
The judges differ, so it is never placed in a ranking with another vendor's number.
Second, a number this guide produced by running the system's own code is marked independently measured.
It sits in its own row.
Third, a retrieval score and an answer score are different quantities.
One asks whether the right passage was found.
The other asks whether the answer came out right.
They never share a table.
This is the single most useful habit a reader can take from the section.

slides.caption: Vendor numbers are flagged and never ranked against each other. Independently measured numbers sit in their own rows. Retrieval scores and answer scores never share a table.

slides.title: Six pages in this *section*
items: Six ways to build a memory

narration: Page two sorts the systems into six classes.
Page three sets out the benchmarks and ten ways a score misleads.
Page four shows why a one-million-token window is not a memory, and what ten million tokens costs.
Page five puts the enterprise workload beside the best results and leaves the question open.
Page six records the one system we reproduced ourselves.
The last page carries every source with its date and its vendor flag.

slides.caption: The six pages: the taxonomy, the benchmarks, long context, the ten-million-token question, what we measured, and the sources.

slides.title: The question is *open*
slides.text: Nothing solid above ten million tokens, from anyone, yet.

narration: No independently run, published result shows any memory architecture answering well over ten million tokens.
No long-context model does either.
None has earned a recommendation, so this section makes none.
It ends on the gap, and leaves the question with you.
Our own research on the question is under way.
It will be published here when it is complete, in the same two tables.

slides.caption: No independently run, published result shows any memory architecture or long-context model answering well over a single ten-million-token corpus. The section ends on that gap.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: High scores are on small tests

narration: Here is what to remember.
A memory is decided by what it stores and when a model runs.
Every high score was earned on a test that fits in one call to a model.
Read every number with its unit, its pool and its judge.
Keep retrieval scores and answer scores apart.
Ten million tokens is the floor for an enterprise memory.
Nothing solid has been shown there, by anyone.
The next page sorts the architectures.

slides.caption: Memory is built by what is stored and when a model runs. Every high score is on a small test. Ten million tokens is the floor, and nothing solid has been shown there.
